At the moment of hatching, the altricial nestling weighs just 1.44 grams [Wwb = 1.44 grams], a remarkably low birth mass that reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the embryo inside the small egg. This neonatal mass is among the lowest recorded for any coraciiform bird of comparable adult size and imposes a heavy demand on the parents, who must begin provisioning the chick almost immediately after the trophic switch to exogenous feeding. Field observations of multiple nests across the Luquillo Mountains indicate that the timing of hatching is tightly synchronized with local insect abundance peaks, ensuring that the parents can secure sufficient prey during the critical first days of the nestling period. The ultimate wet weight for females represents a plateau that is reached after the completion of skeletal development and the full growth of flight feathers. The exact timing of fledging appears to be influenced by the quality and quantity of prey delivered by the parents during the nestling period, with well-fed broods sometimes fledging a day earlier than those receiving less food. Nevertheless, the species-typical fledging age remains remarkably consistent across different years and elevations, suggesting a strong genetic component to the developmental schedule of this species.
